Joseph Keech in Bride's Chair

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Change a right triangle and watch two squares on its legs carve out a smaller square that always fits.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, the two crossing lines, or the circle and its angles.
Look for the math

In 1783 Joseph Keech wrote to a magazine about an old picture: a right triangle with a square built on each leg. Two lines drawn from the sharp corners cut off equal pieces, and those pieces turn out to be the sides of a square tucked inside the triangle.

Why the two cuts are equal

Let the legs have lengths a = AC and b = BC. The far corners of the squares are one quarter turn from C, so AK = BD. The triangle AKL has the same shape as ACF, and BDE has the same shape as BCH: two pairs of similar triangles. Their sides give AK/AC = KL/CF and BD/BC = DE/CH. The first three terms match, so CF = CH. The logic test checks this for every triangle in a grid, not just the opening picture.

The square that fits inside

Draw FZ parallel to AC until it meets the hypotenuse AB at Z. By the same shape argument, CF = FZ, so HCFZ is a square with all four sides equal. Its side is

s = a × b / (a + b)

Turn on "Show statement" to see the two crossing lines and the little marks on the four equal sides. The port keeps the applet's rule that dragging A or B rebuilds the right triangle at C, and that dragging C slides it around its circle; the invariant therefore holds throughout a drag.

Keech's circle and four half-right angles

Keech added a second claim: draw the circle around HCFZ. It meets AB once more at G, and the four angles FGB, FGC, HGC, HGA are each half a right angle. Here G is the foot of the altitude from C, and the little arcs at G show all four angles. The logic test measured them on every non-degenerate case in the grid: all four are 45° to within a millionth of a degree, so the 1783 claim holds. It also found that the circle used by the applet really passes through H, C, F and Z. A translation or rotation of the whole picture changes nothing, because every claim is about a shape, not where it sits on screen.

Try this: tick "Show extra", drag C a long way round its circle, and watch the four arcs stay at 45° while the inner square changes size.
